headline: Exercise reshapes the nerves that run the heart

sources.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen the heart. It rewires it
Regular Exercise Doesn't Just Strengthen the Heart, It Reprograms Its Nerves
Regular exercise may reprogram the nerves that control how the heart beats

chunks.text: Scientists in the United Kingdom have {{come across}} something [[surprising]] about exercise. A team at the University of Bristol {{found out}} that regular aerobic exercise does more than make the heart muscle stronger. It also reshapes the [[tiny]] nerves that {{take care of}} the heart's rhythm. The [[discovery]] could [[lead to]] better care for people with dangerous heartbeat problems.

verbs.correct: To find or discover something by chance
verbs.wrong: To search hard for something over a long time

verbs.correct: To learn something after study or investigation

chunks.text: To find these changes, the team {{set up}} a study on rats. The animals {{worked out}} on a regular plan for ten weeks, a bit like a person going to the gym. Using powerful 3D imaging, the scientists could {{zoom in}} on small clusters of nerve cells near the heart. These cells [[act like]] a dimmer switch that turns the heartbeat up or down.

verbs.correct: To start or organize something new
verbs.wrong: To trick someone into taking the blame

verbs.correct: To do physical exercise to get fit
verbs.wrong: To follow a special diet to lose weight

verbs.correct: To focus closely on one small area to study it
verbs.wrong: To make an image on a screen appear bigger

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very [[unusual]]. On the right side of the heart, the trained rats {{wound up with}} about four times more neurons, the special cells that carry nerve signals. On the left side, the number of cells stayed the same, but each one nearly [[doubled]] in size. Exercise did not shape the two sides in the same way, and that difference intrigued the scientists.

verbs.correct: To happen or be shown to be true in the end
verbs.wrong: To go exactly as the scientists had predicted

verbs.correct: To finally have something as a result
verbs.wrong: To deliberately gather a large amount of something over time

chunks.text: The team hopes these [[findings]] will {{open up}} new ways to [[treat]] heart problems. Doctors already work on these nerves to calm a racing heart, and knowing which side to focus on could make the treatment [[far better]]. This could help people with arrhythmias, chest pain, and other conditions. For now the work is [[at an early stage]], so scientists must {{follow up}} with studies in humans before any therapy is ready.

tf.s: Scientists found out that exercise only makes the heart muscle stronger and nothing else.
tf.why: Exercise also reshapes the tiny nerves that take care of the heart's rhythm, not just the muscle.

tf.s: The team set about their study by training rats for ten weeks.
tf.why: The team set about a study in which the rats worked out on a regular plan for ten weeks.

tf.s: On the right side of the heart, the trained rats wound up with about four times more nerve cells.
tf.why: The story says the trained rats wound up with roughly four times more neurons on the right side.

tf.s: Doctors can already follow up the exercise study with a finished human treatment today.
tf.why: The work is still early, so scientists must follow up with studies in humans before any therapy is ready.

tf.s: The results turned out to be exactly what everyone had expected.
tf.why: The results turned out to be very unusual, since exercise shaped the two sides of the heart differently.

tf.s: The findings could open up new ways to treat heartbeat problems like arrhythmias.
tf.why: The team hopes the findings will open up better, more targeted treatments for arrhythmias and other conditions.
